blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Snap, Google's production-grade networking stack that has been running for over three years, as a groundbreaking departure from traditional TCP/IP-based networking. The paper introduces Pony Express, a transport and communications stack built from scratch to prioritize CPU efficiency and lower latency, rather than reimplementing TCP/IP. The key insight is the need for rapid evolution and deployment of networking enhancements, which Snap achieves by running in user space as a microkernel, enabling weekly releases compared to the months-long cycles of kernel-based solutions. The design leverages shared memory communication, centralized resource accounting, and programmable packet processing, with a focus on dynamic scaling, low tail latency, and compatibility across versions during upgrades. Performance metrics demonstrate significant improvements in throughput, latency, and CPU efficiency over traditional baselines.
paper_title: Snap: a microkernel approach to host networking
paper_abstract: Keywords network stack, datacenter, microkernel, RDMA This paper presents our design and experience with a microkernel-inspired approach to host networking called Snap. Snap is a userspace networking system that supports Google’s rapidly evolving needs with flexible modules that implement a range of network functions, including edge packet switching, virtualization for our cloud platform, traffic shaping policy enforcement, and a high-performance reliable messaging and RDMA-like service. Snap has been running in production for over three years, supporting the extensible communication needs of several large and critical systems. Snap enables fast development and deployment of new networking features, leveraging the benefits of address space isolation and the productivity of userspace software development together with support for transparently upgrading networking services without migrating applications off of a machine. At the same time, Snap achieves compelling performance through a modular architecture that promotes principled synchronization with minimal state sharing, and supports real-time scheduling with dynamic scaling of CPU resources through a novel kernel/userspace CPU scheduler co-design. Our evaluation demonstrates over 3x Gbps/core improvement compared to a kernel networking stack for RPC workloads, software-based RDMA-like performance of up to 5M IOPS/core, and transparent upgrades that are largely imperceptible to user applications. Snap is deployed to over half of our fleet of machines and supports the needs of numerous teams.

figures.title: Three different approaches to organizing networking functionality
figures.caption: Figure 1. Three different approaches to organizing networking functionality: (a) shows a traditional monolithic kernel where applications make system calls, (b) shows a library OS approach without centralization and with application-level thread scheduling of processing, and (c) shows the Snap microkernel-like approach leveraging multicore for fast IPC.
